title: 7 Ways to Manipulate Your Team Into Doing Their Best Work
author: The Good Boss
summary: Gaurav Jain opens with the uncomfortable claim that every leader manipulates, since manipulation at root means influencing behavior, and the real question is whether it is done deliberately and ethically or by accident. He argues that great leaders shape the environment and the systems people work in rather than relying on pressure, personality or speeches. He names seven levers: the environment, what gets measured, the defaults, identity, the narrative, autonomy and consequences. Examples from his own career, a platform modernization, a bug-bounty program that rewarded sloppy code, and a mobile project reframed around meaning, ground each lever. The piece concludes that the line between manipulation and leadership is intent, and invites leaders to audit what behaviors their current system encourages.
points: Behavior changes more reliably through structure and environment than through instructions or speeches.
Metrics are not neutral: measuring hours, tickets or bugs found directs attention, and can incentivize the wrong behavior as with the bug bounty.
Processes act as defaults, so embedding documentation or structured decision-making in the workflow makes disciplined behavior the easy path.
Expectations and framing shape identity and narrative, so describing people as capable and work as meaningful pulls behavior in that direction.
Culture is set by consequences: what is rewarded grows, what is tolerated persists, and what is ignored fades.
quotes: The real question isn’t whether you influence people. You already do. The real question is whether you do it on purpose and in the right way, or by accident.
Speed improved, not because people suddenly became more motivated, but because the system made good behavior easier.
Metrics are not neutral. They quietly shape behavior every day. Choose them carefully.
Instead of asking people to be more disciplined, design workflows that make disciplined behavior the easiest (default) path forward.
If you subtly signal that someone is “still junior,” they will become more cautious of their behavior.
The balance lies in defining outcomes clearly while giving teams freedom over execution. In other words, clarify the WHY and the WHAT, and let your team decide the HOW.
If a high performer who behaves unprofessionally continues to be promoted, the team receives a clear signal that that behavior is acceptable.
